title: TF module stability & signal contracts - exploratory notes
content:
Purpose
This note captures a working approach for making Terraform primitives (VPC, IAM, cluster primitives for EKS/GKE/AKS) resilient during iterative upgrades across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Focus is on: explicit output semantics, stable signal contracts (what downstream layers rely on), and upgrade migration patterns that minimize customer blast radius.

Scope
- VPC primitives (subnets, route tables, NATs, DHCP options labels)
- IAM primitives (roles, policies, service-accounts mapping for cloud and on-prem service users)
- Cluster primitives (EKS/GKE/AKS module interfaces, node pool shapes, taints/labels allowances)
- Outputs and variable contracts which other modules/projects depend on
- Guidance for on-prem/vpc hybrid (customer-managed network pieces)

Why this is important
- We ship private deployments with pinned module versions. Customers copy or reference our modules; small changes can break rollouts if outputs/behaviour mutate.
- Observability/console and automation rely on stable keys/ARN patterns; breaking changes create expensive migrations.

Design principles (short)
1) Minimal surface area: keep public variables/outputs intentionally small. Prefer new optional outputs over changing existing ones.
2) Semantic stability: once an output name is published, maintain it and its format. If a new format required, create a new output name and deprecate the old one in the next major.
3) Explicit signals: add a module-level output called module_contract_version and module_contract_signals (JSON string) describing stable keys. This helps automated consumers.
4) Idempotent upgrades: avoid resource replacement unless approved and documented; provide migration helpers.
5) Cloud-neutral contracts: where possible, outputs should be provider-agnostic (e.g., cluster_endpoint rather than aws_eks_endpoint_arn).

Recommended module surface (example)
- Variables (public):
  - name_prefix (string, required)
  - environment (string, optional, default "dev")
  - create_nat (bool, default true)
  - shared_vpc_id (string, optional) -- for customer-managed VPCs
  - allowed_cidr_blocks (list(string))

- Outputs (public):
  - module_contract_version (string) -- semver-ish for contract, e.g., "1.0.0"
  - module_contract_signals (string) -- small JSON blob describing keys downstream rely on
  - vpc_id (string)
  - public_subnet_ids (list(string))
  - private_subnet_ids (list(string))
  - cluster_endpoint (string) -- provider neutral (API URL for cluster control plane)
  - cluster_ca_certificate (string) -- base64 encoded CA cert data
  - bastion_ip (string) -- optional, empty string when none
  - iam_role_arns (list(string)) -- stable list ordering by role name alphabetical

Signal contract examples
- module_contract_signals -> example value: "{\"vpc\": [\"vpc_id\", \"private_subnet_ids\"], \"cluster\": [\"cluster_endpoint\", \"cluster_ca_certificate\"]}"
- Consumers should parse the JSON and only depend on listed keys. This allows us to add outputs without breaking contracts.

Versioning & compatibility strategy
- Patch (x.y.z): bugfixes internal implementation, no change to outputs or variable meaning.
- Minor (x.y+1.0): add optional variables, add new outputs. Consumers with explicit checks can opt-in to use them.
- Major (x+1.0.0): change semantics or remove outputs. Major bumps require migration playbooks and at least a 4-week deprecation window in our console + changelog.

Upgrade migration patterns
1) Additive approach: for a change that would otherwise alter the format of an output (eg change from single string endpoint to map with ports), add a new output (cluster_endpoint_v2) and keep original. Document mapping.
2) Facade module: provide a thin compatibility module that maps older outputs to newer ones for a release cycle. Example: tf-compat-cluster-outputs module that accepts new outputs and exposes old ones with same names.
3) Safe replacement: if a resource must be replaced (eg change subnet CIDR allocation scheme), provide a dual-stack pattern: create new resources, migrate consumers (DNS endpoints, load balancers) then tear down old. Provide CLI/Terraform example and state move steps.

On-prem considerations
- No ARN semantics: outputs should not use cloud ARNs for internal IDs; use provider-neutral identifiers and include provider metadata when necessary (e.g., provider=aws).
- Network primitives may be customer-managed: if shared_vpc_id provided, module must avoid creating routing changes and instead expose required hooks (route table ids, attachment points) via outputs.
- Kube cluster creation paths differ (kubeadm vs managed). For on-prem, cluster_endpoint should be present but cluster_ca_certificate may be delivered via external secret manager; module should accept reference to secret rather than storing cert as a resource.

EKS/GKE/AKS differences to call out
- node pool semantics: expose node_pool_names (ordered by stable sorting) and node_pool_scaling_config (min/max). Avoid exposing provider generated autoscaler names.
- IAM mapping: on GCP use workload identity references instead of IAM role ARNs. Output should be identity_provider_hint (string) with canonical forms.
- Load balancer addressing: for EKS/GKE we expose lb_ingress_ips (list) and a boolean external_lb. For on-prem, expose ingress_hostname_hint which may be empty.

Testing & CI hooks
- Unit style: terraform validate + fmt + tflint in module CI.
- Integration: nightly apply of module with a minimal example account (non-prod) that asserts public outputs exist and module_contract_version matches expected pattern.
- Upgrade tests: For every minor/major release, CI job which:
  a) applies previous published module version to an account
  b) applies new module over it (module source changed) and runs plan to ensure no unintended destroys
  c) runs a small smoke check that calls cluster_endpoint and attempts kubectl auth (in test harness)

Observability signals and logs
- Module should emit tags/labels for created cloud resources: redwood_module=<name>, redwood_module_version=<version>
- Console expects outputs: billing_tags (map encoded as JSON string) so cost pipeline can attribute resources.
- Add an optional output called tf_plan_checksum which is the sha256 of the last applied plan (stored in state metadata) — useful to detect drift in the console.

Example migration recipe (subnet change)
1) release module that creates new subnets with names <prefix>-private-v2 and outputs private_subnet_ids_v2
2) update application modules to accept private_subnet_ids_v2 when present, otherwise fall back to private_subnet_ids
3) perform gradual rollout of application modules to reference v2 subnets
4) once all consumers moved, run a targeted apply that removes old subnets and then bump module contract version to deprecate old outputs

Documentation/operational checklist (minimum)
- CHANGELOG: record the module_contract_signals patch per release
- MIGRATION_GUIDE.md: for each major change provide a step-by-step migration guide with terraform state mv examples
- Release checklist: run upgrade CI, notify customers in console + slack #priv-deploy-upgrades, open migration ticket for enterprise customers we support

Open questions / items to refine
- Best way to surface module_contract_signals in Redwood Console so that app-level checks can automatically detect incompatible changes.
- Formal format for tf_plan_checksum storage and retention policy.
- Decide default ordering for returned lists (alphabetical by resource name vs creation time). Alphabetical recommended.

Immediate next steps (short actionable)
- Share this note with infra module owners (Diego/Priya) for feedback (week 1)
- Prototype module_contract_signals output across vpc and cluster modules (week 2)
- Add an upgrade CI job template into repo infra-ci (week 3)

References
- RFC-priv-deploy-2024 (link in linked_artifacts)
- GH-PR-3820 (compatibility shim PR)

Notes to self
- Keep the doc minimal; this will become a short Playbook in product docs later. Save migration examples in a separate MIGRATION_GUIDE file to keep this note focused on the contract strategy.
